papers.name: Paper 1P
instructions: Use black ink or ball-point pen.
Fill in the boxes at the top of this page with your name, centre number and candidate number.
Answer the questions in the spaces provided; there may be more space than you need.
Show all the steps in any calculations and state the units.
information: The total mark for this paper is 110.
The marks for each question are shown in brackets; use this as a guide as to how much time to spend on each question.
Where necessary, take the gravitational field strength g to be 10 N/kg.
advice: Read each question carefully before you start to answer it.
Write your answers neatly and in good English.
Check your answers if you have time at the end.
papers.materials: You must have: ruler, protractor, calculator, equation booklet.

sections.title: Answer ALL questions.
sections.instructions: Some questions must be answered with a cross in a box. If you change your mind about an answer, put a line through the box and then mark your new answer with a cross.

papers.name: Paper 2P
instructions: Use black ink or ball-point pen.
Fill in the boxes at the top of this page with your name, centre number and candidate number.
Answer the questions in the spaces provided; there may be more space than you need.
Show all the steps in any calculations and state the units.
information: The total mark for this paper is 70.
The marks for each question are shown in brackets; use this as a guide as to how much time to spend on each question.
Where necessary, take the gravitational field strength g to be 10 N/kg.
advice: Read each question carefully before you start to answer it.
Write your answers neatly and in good English.
Check your answers if you have time at the end.
papers.materials: You must have: ruler, protractor, calculator, equation booklet.

sections.title: Answer ALL questions.
sections.instructions: Some questions must be answered with a cross in a box. If you change your mind about an answer, put a line through the box and then mark your new answer with a cross.

qtypes.label: Multiple choice
qtypes.description: Choose one answer from A-D by putting a cross in a box.

qtypes.label: Recall (state / give / name)
qtypes.description: Short factual answers: state, give, name, identify, complete.

qtypes.label: Describe
qtypes.description: Give an account of a process, pattern, method or observation.

qtypes.label: Explain
qtypes.description: Give reasons linked by physics ideas: point then linked consequence.

qtypes.label: Calculation
qtypes.description: Recall-and-use or given equations: substitution, rearrangement, evaluation, units, unit conversions and significant figures.

qtypes.label: Practical skills and experimental design
qtypes.description: Required practicals: variables, method, measurements, errors, precautions, improvements and processing results.

qtypes.label: Data and graph analysis
qtypes.description: Plot graphs, draw lines of best fit, find gradients and areas, read off values, spot anomalies and draw conclusions.

qtypes.label: Diagrams (circuits, rays, fields, forces)
qtypes.description: Draw or complete circuit diagrams, ray diagrams, field patterns, force diagrams, Sankey diagrams and decay charts.

qtypes.label: Extended response (6 marks)
qtypes.description: Longer structured answer marked with a six-mark levels grid and indicative content.

subtopics.title: Movement and position
subtopics.summary: Speed, velocity and acceleration; distance-time and velocity-time graphs; the v^2 = u^2 + 2as equation.

points.summary: Work in kg, m, m/s, m/s², N, s and N/kg.
Draw and interpret graphs of distance against time.
Average speed is distance moved divided by time taken.
Practical: measure the motion of everyday objects such as toy cars or balls.
Acceleration is change in velocity divided by time taken.
Draw and interpret graphs of velocity against time.
The gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.
The area under a velocity-time graph gives distance travelled.
Use v² = u² + 2as for uniform acceleration.

subtopics.title: Forces, weight and stopping
subtopics.summary: What forces do, vectors and scalars, resultant force, F = ma, weight, stopping distance and terminal velocity.

points.summary: Forces can change an object's speed, shape or direction.
Recognise kinds of force such as gravitational, electrostatic, friction and drag.
Vectors have size and direction; scalars have size only.
Force is a vector.
Add forces acting along one line to find the resultant.
Friction acts against motion.
Resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Weight equals mass times gravitational field strength.
Stopping distance is thinking distance plus braking distance.
Speed, mass, road surface and reaction time change stopping distance.
Weight and drag on a falling object; why it reaches terminal velocity.

subtopics.title: Stretching springs and materials
subtopics.summary: Force-extension investigations for springs, wires and rubber bands; Hooke's law region; elastic behaviour.

points.summary: Practical: measure how extension depends on the load for springs, wires and rubber bands.
The first straight part of a force-extension graph shows Hooke's law.
An elastic material returns to its original shape once the load is removed.

subtopics.title: Momentum and Newton's third law
subtopics.summary: Momentum p = mv, conservation in collisions and explosions, force as rate of change of momentum, safety features, third law pairs.

points.summary: Work in N m and kg m/s.
Momentum equals mass times velocity.
Use momentum ideas to explain crumple zones, airbags and helmets.
Use conservation of momentum to find masses or velocities.
Force equals change in momentum divided by time taken.
Newton's third law: interacting bodies exert equal and opposite forces on each other.

subtopics.title: Moments and centre of gravity
subtopics.summary: Moment = force x perpendicular distance, principle of moments, centre of gravity, forces on a supported beam.

points.summary: Moment equals force times perpendicular distance from the pivot.
An object's weight acts through its centre of gravity.
Balanced objects: clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments.
How the support forces on a light beam change as a heavy load moves along it.

subtopics.title: Mains electricity and electrical power
subtopics.summary: Safety features (insulation, earthing, fuses, circuit breakers), heating effect, P = IV, E = IVt, fuse choice, a.c. and d.c.

points.summary: Work in A, C, J, Ω, s, V and W.
How insulation, double insulation, earthing, fuses and circuit breakers protect people and appliances.
Current in a resistor heats it; uses of this heating at home.
Power equals current times voltage; choose the right fuse.
Energy transferred equals current times voltage times time.
Mains is alternating current; cells and batteries give direct current.

subtopics.title: Circuits, resistance and components
subtopics.summary: Series and parallel circuits, I-V characteristics, LDRs and thermistors, V = IR, lamps and LEDs as indicators.

points.summary: Choose series or parallel circuits for a job, e.g. house lighting.
In series, current depends on the supply voltage and on the components in the loop.
Current-voltage behaviour of wires, resistors, filament lamps and diodes, and how to measure it.
More resistance means less current.
LDR resistance falls as light gets brighter; thermistor resistance falls as it gets hotter.
A lamp or LED can show that a current is flowing.
Voltage equals current times resistance.

subtopics.title: Charge, current and voltage
subtopics.summary: Current as rate of flow of charge, Q = It, electrons in metals, junction rule, parallel voltages, series calculations, E = QV.

points.summary: Current is how quickly charge flows.
Charge equals current times time.
In metal wires the current is a flow of electrons.
Current into a junction equals current out because charge is conserved.
Components in parallel have the same voltage across them.
Work out currents, voltages and resistances for two components in series.
Voltage is energy per unit charge; one volt is one joule per coulomb.
Energy transferred equals charge times voltage.

subtopics.title: Electrostatics
subtopics.summary: Conductors and insulators, charging by friction, electron transfer, attraction and repulsion, dangers and uses of static.

points.summary: Name common conductors (metals) and insulators (plastics).
Practical: charge insulating materials by rubbing them.
Objects become charged by gaining electrons (negative) or losing electrons (positive).
Unlike charges attract and like charges repel.
Explain static effects using the movement of electrons.
Dangers of static, e.g. sparks when refuelling aircraft and tankers.
Uses of static, e.g. photocopiers and inkjet printers.

subtopics.title: Properties of waves
subtopics.summary: Transverse and longitudinal waves, wave terms, v = fλ, f = 1/T, Doppler effect, reflection and refraction.

points.summary: Work in degrees, Hz, m, m/s and s.
Difference between longitudinal and transverse waves.
Meaning of amplitude, wavefront, frequency, wavelength and period.
Waves carry energy and information but not matter.
Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
Frequency equals one divided by the time period.
Apply the wave equations to sound and electromagnetic waves.
Doppler effect: a moving source changes the observed frequency and wavelength.
All waves can be reflected and refracted.

subtopics.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
subtopics.summary: Order of the spectrum, same speed in a vacuum, uses of each region, harmful effects and protection.

points.summary: Light is one part of a continuous EM spectrum; all EM waves travel at the same speed in space.
Order the spectrum by wavelength and frequency, including the colours of visible light.
Uses of radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.
Harm from too much microwave, infrared, ultraviolet and gamma exposure, and ways to reduce it.

subtopics.title: Light: reflection, refraction and total internal reflection
subtopics.summary: Law of reflection, ray diagrams, refraction practicals, n = sin i / sin r, critical angle and optical fibres.

points.summary: Light is a transverse wave that reflects and refracts.
Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
Draw ray diagrams for reflection and refraction.
Practical: trace rays through rectangular and semicircular blocks and prisms.
Refractive index equals sin i divided by sin r.
Practical: find the refractive index of a glass block.
Total internal reflection in optical fibres and prisms.
What the critical angle means.
sin c equals 1 divided by the refractive index.

subtopics.title: Sound
subtopics.summary: Sound as a longitudinal wave, hearing range, measuring the speed of sound, oscilloscope traces, pitch and loudness.

points.summary: Sound is a longitudinal wave that reflects and refracts.
Humans hear from about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
Practical: measure the speed of sound in air.
Use a microphone and oscilloscope to display a sound wave.
Practical: find the frequency of a sound from an oscilloscope trace.
Higher frequency of vibration gives a higher pitch.
Larger amplitude of vibration gives a louder sound.

subtopics.title: Energy stores, transfers and efficiency
subtopics.summary: Energy stores and transfer pathways, conservation of energy, efficiency and Sankey diagrams.

points.summary: Work in kg, J, m, m/s, m/s², N, s and W.
Name energy stores and the ways energy is transferred between them.
Energy is never created or destroyed.
Efficiency is useful energy output divided by total energy output (times 100%).
Describe energy transfers in devices and draw Sankey diagrams.

subtopics.title: Thermal energy transfer
subtopics.summary: Conduction, convection and radiation, convection currents, surfaces and radiation, investigations and insulation.

points.summary: Thermal energy moves by conduction, convection and radiation.
Convection explains sea breezes, room heating and similar effects.
How surface colour, texture and temperature affect emission and absorption of radiation.
Practical: investigate conduction, convection and radiation.
Reduce unwanted energy transfer using insulation and other methods.

subtopics.title: Work, energy and power
subtopics.summary: W = Fd, work as energy transferred, GPE = mgh, KE = ½mv², energy conservation in falling and rising objects, P = W/t.

points.summary: Work done equals force times distance moved in the direction of the force.
Work done is the same as energy transferred.
Gravitational potential energy equals mgh.
Kinetic energy equals half times mass times speed squared.
Link GPE, KE and work using conservation of energy.
Power is the rate of transferring energy or doing work.
Power equals work done divided by time taken.

subtopics.title: Energy resources and electricity generation
subtopics.summary: Energy transfers in power stations and renewable generators; advantages and disadvantages of each resource.

points.summary: Energy transfers when electricity is generated from wind, water, geothermal, solar, fossil and nuclear sources.
Compare renewable and non-renewable large-scale electricity generation.

subtopics.title: Density and pressure
subtopics.summary: ρ = m/V and how to measure it, p = F/A, pressure in fluids acting in all directions, p = hρg.

points.summary: Work in °C, K, J, kg, kg/m³, m, m², m³, m/s, m/s², N and Pa.
Density equals mass divided by volume.
Practical: find density from measured mass and volume.
Pressure equals force divided by area.
Pressure at a point in a still fluid acts equally in all directions.
Pressure difference equals height times density times g.

subtopics.title: Change of state and specific heat capacity
subtopics.summary: Particle models of solids, liquids and gases, heating and changes of state, cooling curves, ΔQ = mcΔT and SHC practicals.

points.summary: Work in J/kg °C.
Heating raises the internal energy, so temperature rises or the state changes.
What happens to particles during melting, evaporation and boiling.
Arrangement and motion of particles in solids, liquids and gases.
Practical: get a temperature-time graph showing a flat section during a change of state.
Specific heat capacity: energy to warm 1 kg by 1 °C.
Change in thermal energy equals m × c × ΔT.
Practical: measure the specific heat capacity of water and solids.

subtopics.title: Ideal gas molecules
subtopics.summary: Molecular motion and gas pressure, absolute zero and the Kelvin scale, p1V1 = p2V2 and p1/T1 = p2/T2.

points.summary: Gas molecules move randomly and hit the walls, causing a force and so a pressure.
Why there is an absolute zero at -273 °C.
Convert between Kelvin and Celsius temperatures.
Higher temperature means faster gas molecules on average.
Kelvin temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
Explain how pressure depends on volume (fixed T) and on Kelvin temperature (fixed V).
Use p1/T1 = p2/T2 for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume.
Use p1V1 = p2V2 for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature.

subtopics.title: Magnets and magnetic fields
subtopics.summary: Attraction and repulsion, hard and soft magnetic materials, field lines, induced magnetism, plotting fields, uniform fields.

points.summary: Work in A, V and W.
Magnets attract or repel other magnets and attract magnetic materials.
Hard magnetic materials keep magnetism; soft ones lose it easily.
Meaning of a magnetic field line.
Some materials become magnets when placed in a magnetic field.
Practical: plot the field around one bar magnet and between two.
Use two magnets to make a uniform field.

subtopics.title: Electromagnetism and the motor effect
subtopics.summary: Fields around currents, electromagnets, force on moving charges and currents in fields, left-hand rule, motors and loudspeakers.

points.summary: A current in a wire makes a magnetic field around it.
How an electromagnet is built.
Field patterns for a straight wire, a flat coil and a solenoid.
A charged particle moving across a magnetic field feels a force.
Why a current-carrying wire in a field feels a force; d.c. motors and loudspeakers.
Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force.
Size and direction of the force depend on the current and field.

subtopics.title: Electromagnetic induction and generators
subtopics.summary: Inducing a voltage by moving a conductor or changing a field; generators; factors affecting the induced voltage.

points.summary: A voltage is induced when a conductor cuts field lines or the field through a coil changes; what makes it bigger.
Generating electricity by spinning a magnet in a coil or a coil in a field.

subtopics.title: Transformers and transmission
subtopics.summary: Transformer structure, step-up and step-down use in the grid, turns-ratio equation and VpIp = VsIs.

points.summary: A transformer has two coils on an iron core and changes the size of an alternating voltage.
Step-up and step-down transformers in power transmission.
Vp/Vs = Np/Ns.
For a 100% efficient transformer, input power equals output power: VpIp = VsIs.

subtopics.title: Atoms and nuclear radiation
subtopics.summary: Atomic structure and nuclide notation, isotopes, alpha, beta, gamma and neutron emission, nuclear equations and detectors.

points.summary: Work in Bq, cm, h, min and s.
Protons, neutrons and electrons; nuclide symbols such as carbon-14.
Atomic number, mass number and isotope.
Alpha, beta and gamma are ionising radiations emitted randomly by unstable nuclei.
What alpha, beta and gamma are; their penetration and ionising power.
Practical: compare penetrating power using sources or a simulation.
How alpha, beta, gamma and neutron emission change atomic and mass numbers.
Balance nuclear equations for mass and charge.
Photographic film and Geiger-Müller tubes detect ionising radiation.

subtopics.title: Activity, half-life, uses and dangers
subtopics.summary: Background radiation, activity in Bq, half-life calculations and graphs, uses, contamination and irradiation, dangers and waste.

points.summary: Sources of background radiation from the Earth and from space.
Activity falls with time and is measured in becquerels.
Half-life is the time for activity (or undecayed nuclei) to halve; it differs between isotopes.
Half-life calculations, including reading graphs.
Uses of radioactivity in medicine and industry.
Contamination versus irradiation.
Radiation damages cells and causes mutations; risks of radioactive waste and how to reduce them.

subtopics.title: Fission and fusion
subtopics.summary: Fission of U-235 and chain reactions, control rods, moderators and shielding, fusion in stars and why it needs extreme conditions.

points.summary: Fission, fusion and decay all release energy.
A neutron hitting U-235 makes it split, releasing kinetic energy of the products.
Fission gives two radioactive daughter nuclei and two or three neutrons.
Released neutrons can cause further fissions: a chain reaction.
Control rods absorb neutrons; the moderator slows them down.
Shielding around the reactor absorbs radiation.
Fusion joins nuclei; fission splits them.
Fusion makes a heavier nucleus with a small loss of mass and releases energy.
Stars are powered by fusion.
Fusion needs very high temperature and pressure to overcome repulsion between protons.

subtopics.title: Motion in the universe
subtopics.summary: Universe, galaxies and the Milky Way, gravitational field strength on different bodies, orbits of planets, moons, comets and satellites, v = 2πr/T.

points.summary: Work in kg, m, m/s, m/s², N, s and N/kg.
The universe contains billions of galaxies; a galaxy contains billions of stars; we are in the Milky Way.
Why g differs between the Earth, the Moon and other planets.
Gravity keeps moons, planets, satellites and comets in orbit.
Compare the orbits of comets, moons and planets.
Orbital speed equals 2πr divided by the time period.

subtopics.title: Stellar evolution and the HR diagram
subtopics.summary: Star colour and temperature, life cycles of Sun-like and massive stars, absolute magnitude and the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.

points.summary: Stars can be sorted by colour.
A star's colour depends on its surface temperature.
Life cycle of a Sun-like star: nebula, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf.
Life cycle of stars much more massive than the Sun.
Absolute magnitude describes brightness at a standard distance.
Sketch the main parts of the HR diagram.

subtopics.title: Cosmology and red-shift
subtopics.summary: Big Bang theory, red-shift and CMB evidence, Doppler shift and Δλ/λ0 = v/c, expansion of the universe.

points.summary: How the universe has evolved and why the Big Bang theory is supported.
Evidence for the Big Bang: red-shift and cosmic microwave background radiation.
A moving source changes the observed frequency and wavelength.
Δλ/λ0 = v/c links wavelength change to a galaxy's speed.
More distant galaxies show bigger red-shifts.
Red-shift shows that the universe is expanding.
